report:
**Conclusion: No.** The best clinical evidence does not show that coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) improves Parkinson’s movement symptoms or slows the disease.

Why the answer can seem like “yes”: a small, early phase-II trial in untreated early Parkinson’s suggested a possible dose-related slowing of worsening on the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS). That was a preliminary signal—not proof—and prompted the larger QE3 study.

The decisive follow-up was a phase-III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 67 North American sites in people with early Parkinson’s. It tested high-dose CoQ10 (1,200 or 2,400 mg/day) plus vitamin E versus placebo. The trial was stopped early for futility: CoQ10 did **not** improve clinical progression, including the UPDRS measures that capture motor impairment and daily functioning. Thus, it provides no evidence of a meaningful benefit for movement disorder symptoms or neuroprotection. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/?dopt=Abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/?dopt=Abstract)

A systematic review of CoQ10 in Parkinsonian syndromes likewise describes mixed early studies but concludes that clinical evidence is insufficient/negative for Parkinson’s disease, despite plausible antioxidant and mitochondrial mechanisms. Biological plausibility and animal-model findings do not establish patient benefit. [https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975)

CoQ10 was generally tolerated in the major trial, but “safe” is not the same as effective. It should not replace proven Parkinson’s treatments (such as levodopa and appropriate exercise/physical therapy). Discuss supplements with the treating neurologist, especially because product quality, cost, and interactions with an individual’s medications matter. The original trial registration confirms the study was designed to test whether CoQ10 slowed early-Parkinson’s decline. [https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00740714](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00740714)
